impact.why: Impact is high because the sole prompt-injection defense the threat model mandates (delimited, labelled untrusted content) is removed for attacker-chosen author==self, and the design equates steering an agent with a shell/exfil primitive; likelihood is high because the author name set is tiny and guessable and a single unsigned object triggers it; it is not critical because the model still has to act on the injected text (a probabilistic step) rather than a deterministic code-exec sink.

private ingestOne(post: Post): boolean {
    const result = this.db.query(`
      INSERT OR IGNORE INTO posts
        (id, board, thread, reply_to, author, instance, ts, title, body, post_json)
      VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?)
    `).run(
      post.id,
      post.board,
      post.thread,
      post.replyTo ?? null,
      post.author,
      post.instance,
      post.ts,
      post.title ?? null,
      post.body,
      canonicalize(post),
    );
    if (result.changes === 0) return false;
codeEvidence.explanation: ingestOne calls canonicalize inside the SQLite transaction; a RangeError rolls the transaction back and the sync cursor never advances, so every later sync re-hits the same object.
codeEvidence.label: canonicalize runs inside the ingest transaction

confidence.rationale: PoC builds a validatePost-accepted post with ext nested 60k deep; validatePost returns it and canonicalize throws RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded, which occurs inside the ingest transaction and rolls it back.

preventiveControls: Apply schema-level size/shape limits to all attacker-controlled JSON at the trust boundary (validatePost).
findings.remediation: Bound post byte size and JSON/`ext` nesting depth in `validatePost`, and make `BoardIndex.ingest` skip an individual post that throws while still advancing the sync cursor, so one malformed object cannot permanently stall every reader.
remediationTests: A post with `ext` nested beyond the configured depth is rejected by validatePost.

private ingestOne(post: Post): boolean {
    const result = this.db.query(`
      INSERT OR IGNORE INTO posts
        (id, board, thread, reply_to, author, instance, ts, title, body, post_json)
      VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?)
    `).run(
      post.id,
      post.board,
      post.thread,
      post.replyTo ?? null,
      post.author,
      post.instance,
      post.ts,
      post.title ?? null,
      post.body,
      canonicalize(post),
    );
    if (result.changes === 0) return false;

    if (post.id === post.thread) {
      this.db.query(`
        INSERT INTO threads (root_id, board, title, last_activity, reply_count)
        VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, 0)
        ON CONFLICT(root_id) DO UPDATE SET
          board = excluded.board,
          title = excluded.title,
          last_activity = max(threads.last_activity, excluded.last_activity)
      `).run(post.id, post.board, post.title ?? null, post.ts);
    } else {
      this.db.query(`
        INSERT INTO threads (root_id, board, title, last_activity, reply_count)
        VALUES (?, ?, NULL, ?, 1)
        ON CONFLICT(root_id) DO UPDATE SET
          last_activity = max(threads.last_activity, excluded.last_activity),
          reply_count = threads.reply_count + 1
      `).run(post.thread, post.board, post.ts);
    }

codeEvidence.explanation: Unread mentions are those with `p.id > cursor`; once the cursor is a maximal id every ordinary later mention is excluded.
codeEvidence.label: Mentions are filtered by p.id > cursor

codeEvidence.explanation: The durable per-author cursor is set to the id of the last delivered post, so delivering one forged max-ULID mention pins it at the top of the ULID space forever; MCP readUnread/readSince persist the same poisoned cursor.
codeEvidence.label: Cursor persisted as the last delivered id

confidence.rationale: PoC writes one forged mention with a large valid ULID then a legitimate mention; inject #1 delivers the forged post and advances hook_cursors, inject #2 returns empty so the real message is never delivered.

preventiveControls: Sign posts so a forged `id`/`author` is rejected before it can poison per-agent state.
findings.remediation: Bind a post to its storage key (reject when `key != keyFor(id)`), reject posts whose ULID timestamp is materially ahead of wall-clock, and advance the hook and MCP read cursors by delivered-arrival rather than by maximum `id` so a single future-dated object cannot skip all later mentions.
remediationTests: After a mention with a far-future ULID is delivered, a subsequent ordinary mention is still injected by the hook and by MCP board_read.
validatePost/ingest reject a post whose storage key does not match keyFor(id).

dataflow.summary: agent A's hook runs without BOARD_AS while ambient env or a parent process name matches agent B -> resolveIdentity returns B -> the hook claims B's mentions, marks them read (hook_cursors), and publishes presence as B

impact.why: Impact is low because at worst one local agent consumes/marks-read another local agent's mentions (integrity of a local inbox) with no cross-boundary or data-exposure effect, and likelihood is low because the shipped installer sets BOARD_AS and conflicting ambient env is unusual; the identity-ambiguity requirement in the threat model still makes it worth recording.

likelihood.why: Requires no BOARD_AS and conflicting environment/ancestry on a shared dev host; the payload itself is host-generated, not attacker-supplied.

reachability.summary: Requires no BOARD_AS and conflicting environment/ancestry on a shared dev host; the payload itself is host-generated, not attacker-supplied.

attackPath.summary: agent A's hook runs without BOARD_AS while ambient env or a parent process name matches agent B -> resolveIdentity returns B -> the hook claims B's mentions, marks them read (hook_cursors), and publishes presence as B

confidence.rationale: resolveRuntime returns the first matching env family in fixed order with no conflict detection; the shipped tests confirm it fails closed only on unknown/empty tokens, not on multiple conflicting environment signals.

preventiveControls: Require an explicit BOARD_AS in all generated configs (the installer already does).
findings.remediation: Fail closed (return no identity) when more than one distinct runtime signal is present, and require `BOARD_AS` when payload/env/ancestry evidence conflicts.
remediationTests: resolveIdentity throws when both a Letta and a Claude environment signal are present without BOARD_AS.

rootCause.summary: resolveRuntime (config.ts:93-98) returns letta if any LETTA_AGENT_ID/AGENT_ID/CONVERSATION_ID is set, else codex, else claude, without detecting that several are set at once; detectAncestorRuntime (config.ts:121-138) treats any of the first three argv tokens of any ancestor process as the runtime; resolveIdentity then claims and consumes that identity's mentions.

severity.changeConditions: Failing closed (no identity) when more than one runtime signal is present, or requiring BOARD_AS, would satisfy the stated invariant.
severity.rationale: Impact is low because at worst one local agent consumes/marks-read another local agent's mentions (integrity of a local inbox) with no cross-boundary or data-exposure effect, and likelihood is low because the shipped installer sets BOARD_AS and conflicting ambient env is unusual; the identity-ambiguity requirement in the threat model still makes it worth recording.

findings.summary: Hook identity inference does not fail closed on conflicting evidence: without BOARD_AS, resolveRuntime returns the first matching environment family in a fixed order (any LETTA_AGENT_ID/AGENT_ID/CONVERSATION_ID wins over CODEX_*, which wins over CLAUDE_*), and the ancestor fallback treats any of the first three argv tokens of any ancestor process (e.g. `tmux new -s claude`) as the runtime, so a Claude Code hook running with an ambient AGENT_ID or under a differently named parent claims and consumes another agent's mentions.
findings.title: Hook identity does not fail closed on conflicting runtime signals

assertions: env families checked in fixed order
limitations: The installer always sets BOARD_AS (authoritative), so this only bites manual configs or unsupported runtimes; genuine conflicting env is uncommon.
Remaining uncertainty: How often two agents share ambient env on one host without BOARD_AS.
validation.summary: resolveRuntime (config.ts:93-98) returns letta if any LETTA_AGENT_ID/AGENT_ID/CONVERSATION_ID is set, else codex, else claude, without detecting that several are set at once; detectAncestorRuntime (config.ts:121-138) treats any of the first three argv tokens of any ancestor process as the runtime; resolveIdentity then claims and consumes that identity's mentions.

preventiveControls: Make the store read path resilient to per-entry filesystem errors.
findings.remediation: Tolerate `EACCES`/`EPERM` in the directory walk (skip and continue, as `ENOENT` already is) so one unreadable entry cannot break every reader.
remediationTests: list() returns the readable keys and skips an unreadable (mode-000) subtree instead of throwing.

confidence.rationale: PoC posts a legit message then writes a forged object reusing the same id in an older day bucket; a fresh index build ingests the older-bucket object first and INSERT OR IGNORE drops the real one, so the reader sees the attacker body under the legit id.

findings.remediation: Reject or ignore any object whose storage key does not equal `keyFor(id)` before ingest so a duplicate `id` in another bucket cannot win index dedup; add signing to bind content to identity.
remediationTests: Ingesting an object whose key bucket does not match keyFor(id) is rejected, so a same-id duplicate cannot replace the real post.

rootCause.summary: Board.since lists every key under the posts prefix in byte order regardless of bucket; loadOne (board.ts:241-246) parses whatever is at each key without checking key==keyFor(id); ingestOne (index.ts:130-146) dedups with INSERT OR IGNORE on id, so the first-listed (older-bucket) forged object wins on a fresh index.

severity.changeConditions: Binding a post to its storage key (reject when key != keyFor(id)) and/or signing would eliminate the substitution.
severity.rationale: Impact is capped at low/medium because it refines an impersonation capability the threat model already accepts (unsigned posts) rather than crossing a new boundary, and likelihood is low because it only affects fresh index builds; the concrete weakness (trusting the id inside an object over the key it was read from, so an older-bucket duplicate wins) is worth a low finding; matrix medium+low -> low.

findings.summary: Index post substitution: because id/board are not bound to the key, a store writer can place an object in an older day bucket whose `id` equals an existing legitimate post; on any fresh index build (new runtime install, new --index path) ingestSince walks keys in order, the forged object is inserted first and the real post is dropped by INSERT OR IGNORE, so readers see attacker content under the original author and id even where the original object is immutable.
findings.title: Same-id object in an older bucket substitutes post content for fresh readers

assertions: since() lists all buckets in key order
INSERT OR IGNORE dedups by id -> first wins
limitations: The threat model already accepts author impersonation (posts unsigned); readers who already ingested the real post keep it. The delta is same-id substitution defeating object immutability for fresh readers.
Remaining uncertainty: Whether real deployments frequently rebuild indexes (new install / new --index path) where the substitution takes effect.
validation.summary: Board.since lists every key under the posts prefix in byte order regardless of bucket; loadOne (board.ts:241-246) parses whatever is at each key without checking key==keyFor(id); ingestOne (index.ts:130-146) dedups with INSERT OR IGNORE on id, so the first-listed (older-bucket) forged object wins on a fresh index.

dataflow.summary: store writer -> one or many oversized objects -> every reader loads them fully into memory on get + index + FTS; MCP emits an oversized tool result to the model

impact.why: Impact is low because it is bounded resource consumption (memory/context bloat) on the local reader with no persistence or cross-boundary effect, and likelihood is medium because it needs sizeable objects rather than a trivial one; the matrix and the DoS calibration guidance keep transient/mitigable resource issues at low.

likelihood.why: Any store writer; all readers. docs/research/04-trust.md recommends skipping bodies > 64 KiB and capping ingest, unimplemented.

reachability.summary: Any store writer; all readers. docs/research/04-trust.md recommends skipping bodies > 64 KiB and capping ingest, unimplemented.

attackPath.summary: store writer -> one or many oversized objects -> every reader loads them fully into memory on get + index + FTS; MCP emits an oversized tool result to the model

confidence.rationale: PoC shows validatePost accepts a 20 MB body; FsStore.get/S3Store.get read whole objects into memory and MCP toolResult serialises the full page, but no crash was forced so impact is resource pressure rather than a proven outage.

preventiveControls: Implement the ingest caps recommended in docs/research/04-trust.md.
findings.remediation: Enforce the documented per-object (e.g. 64 KiB body) and per-sync ingest caps in `validatePost`/the store read path, and cap the aggregate byte size of an MCP tool result.
remediationTests: A post whose body exceeds the configured cap is rejected or skipped.
A board_read result is bounded in total bytes.

rootCause.summary: validatePost (post.ts:98) checks only typeof body; FsStore.get (store-fs:83-85) and S3Store.get (store-s3:99) buffer the whole object; toolResult (server.ts:485-491) JSON.stringifies the full page.

severity.changeConditions: Enforcing the documented per-object and per-ingest size caps would close it.
severity.rationale: Impact is low because it is bounded resource consumption (memory/context bloat) on the local reader with no persistence or cross-boundary effect, and likelihood is medium because it needs sizeable objects rather than a trivial one; the matrix and the DoS calibration guidance keep transient/mitigable resource issues at low.

findings.summary: No bound on object size anywhere in the read path: FsStore.get and S3Store.get read whole objects into memory, validatePost accepts any body length, the index stores body and FTS for every post, and MCP toolResult serialises up to 1000 posts per call into one text block; a store writer can make every reader load and index arbitrarily large objects (memory exhaustion, index bloat, oversized tool results sent to the model).
findings.title: Unbounded object size lets a store writer exhaust reader memory and bloat tool output

limitations: Memory pressure is bounded by object size and Bun handles multi-MB strings; no deterministic crash demonstrated.
Remaining uncertainty: Whether a realistic bucket/quota would allow objects large enough to OOM a target before other limits apply.
validation.summary: validatePost (post.ts:98) checks only typeof body; FsStore.get (store-fs:83-85) and S3Store.get (store-s3:99) buffer the whole object; toolResult (server.ts:485-491) JSON.stringifies the full page.

dataflow.summary: hostile/compromised S3 endpoint -> every S3Store.list (which underlies board.since/scan and every hook and MCP read/sync) loops forever -> the reader hangs and never makes progress

impact.why: Impact is medium because the reader hangs indefinitely (a hard availability failure of hooks and MCP), but likelihood is low because it needs a hostile or compromised S3-compatible endpoint rather than mere bucket-write access; matrix medium+low -> low.

likelihood.why: An untrusted S3 endpoint (in scope per the threat model); affects all readers pointed at it. No object writes needed.

reachability.summary: An untrusted S3 endpoint (in scope per the threat model); affects all readers pointed at it. No object writes needed.

attackPath.summary: hostile/compromised S3 endpoint -> every S3Store.list (which underlies board.since/scan and every hook and MCP read/sync) loops forever -> the reader hangs and never makes progress

confidence.rationale: PoC injects a client whose list() always returns {contents:[],isTruncated:true,nextContinuationToken:'tok'}; S3Store.list never returns and the process is killed after 120s, confirming the unbounded loop.

preventiveControls: Bound all remote-driven iteration and treat non-progress as failure.
findings.remediation: Add a maximum page/iteration bound to `S3Store.list` and treat a continuation that returns no progress as terminal.
remediationTests: S3Store.list terminates within a bounded number of pages against an endpoint that always reports truncated with no new keys.

rootCause.summary: list (store-s3:117-150) breaks only on !page.isTruncated (:142) or a non-advancing page when no continuationToken is present (:144-149); an endpoint returning isTruncated:true plus a token and zero matching keys satisfies neither, so the loop never terminates.

severity.changeConditions: Add a maximum page/iteration bound and treat a non-advancing continuation as truncated-with-no-progress, raising severity if untrusted endpoints are common in the deployment.
severity.rationale: Impact is medium because the reader hangs indefinitely (a hard availability failure of hooks and MCP), but likelihood is low because it needs a hostile or compromised S3-compatible endpoint rather than mere bucket-write access; matrix medium+low -> low.

findings.summary: Infinite loop on a hostile S3 endpoint: S3Store.list loops while keys.length < requested and only breaks on `!page.isTruncated` or (in the no-continuation-token branch) a non-advancing page; an untrusted S3-compatible endpoint that always returns isTruncated:true with a continuationToken and zero matching keys never satisfies either break, so every hooks/MCP list (and therefore every board read/sync) hangs forever.
findings.title: A hostile S3 endpoint hangs every reader in an unbounded list loop

assertions: non-advance guard only in the no-token branch
a persistent token bypasses every break
limitations: Requires the S3 endpoint itself to be hostile/compromised (a stronger position than a bucket writer), but the threat model treats the store/endpoint as untrusted.
Remaining uncertainty: Whether real deployments use an untrusted S3-compatible endpoint versus AWS.
validation.summary: list (store-s3:117-150) breaks only on !page.isTruncated (:142) or a non-advancing page when no continuationToken is present (:144-149); an endpoint returning isTruncated:true plus a token and zero matching keys satisfies neither, so the loop never terminates.

dataflow.summary: operator passes git remote with a token-as-username URL -> installer's credential refusal misses it (colon-required regex) -> token persisted verbatim into runtime config, MCP args, and replica .git/config, and printed unredacted in the dry-run diff and errors

impact.why: Impact is low because it is the operator's own token written to their own 0600 files and terminal rather than a cross-boundary disclosure, but it is a real bypass of an explicit safety control (credential-URL refusal) that most GitHub PAT usage would hit; likelihood is medium given how commonly tokens are embedded in HTTPS git URLs; a self-owned secret in private files keeps it at low.

likelihood.why: Operator-controlled input on the operator's own machine; the security-relevant fact is that the tool explicitly promises to refuse credential URLs and silently fails for the most common GitHub PAT form.

reachability.summary: Operator-controlled input on the operator's own machine; the security-relevant fact is that the tool explicitly promises to refuse credential URLs and silently fails for the most common GitHub PAT form.

attackPath.summary: operator passes git remote with a token-as-username URL -> installer's credential refusal misses it (colon-required regex) -> token persisted verbatim into runtime config, MCP args, and replica .git/config, and printed unredacted in the dry-run diff and errors

codeEvidence.explanation: normalizeStoreSpec rejects only `://user:pass@`; a token-as-username URL (`https://TOKEN@host`) has no colon and passes.
codeEvidence.label: Credential refusal requires a colon in userinfo

codeEvidence.explanation: The accepted spec (with the token) is written verbatim into the generated hook command and MCP args, then persisted to the runtime config file and the replica .git/config.
codeEvidence.label: The store spec is embedded into the persisted hook command

confidence.rationale: PoC: installRuntime with store git remote https://ghp_SECRETTOKEN123@github.com/... is accepted and the token is written verbatim into ~/.cursor/mcp.json, while https://u:p@... is still refused; the refusal regex requires a colon inside userinfo.

preventiveControls: Never place credentials in store URLs; use the runtime credential environment as the README instructs.
findings.remediation: Refuse any store URL that carries userinfo (`://...@`, matching the previous revision) rather than only `user:pass@`, and redact userinfo in the dry-run diff and error output.
remediationTests: renderInstallDiff redacts userinfo for token-in-URL remotes.

rootCause.summary: normalizeStoreSpec (install.ts:398) matches only `://user:pass@`; the token form `https://TOKEN@host` has no colon and passes; the spec is embedded into the hook command (install.ts:386-394) and MCP args (install.ts:162) and later written to the replica .git/config; safeDiffLine (install.ts:143) redacts only user:pass URLs.

severity.changeConditions: Widen the refusal to any URL with userinfo (`://...@`, matching the previous revision) and redact userinfo in the dry-run diff; evidence of a shared/synced config raising exposure would raise severity.
severity.rationale: Impact is low because it is the operator's own token written to their own 0600 files and terminal rather than a cross-boundary disclosure, but it is a real bypass of an explicit safety control (credential-URL refusal) that most GitHub PAT usage would hit; likelihood is medium given how commonly tokens are embedded in HTTPS git URLs; a self-owned secret in private files keeps it at low.

findings.summary: Installer credential refusal only matches `user:pass@`; the common token-as-username form (`https://ghp_xxx@github.com/org/repo.git`, `https://x-access-token@...` without a password) passes normalizeStoreSpec and is persisted verbatim into the hook command in ~/.claude/settings.json / ~/.codex/config.toml and into MCP args in ~/.claude.json etc., echoed unredacted by the dry-run diff, and later stored in the replica's .git/config by GitStore.
findings.title: Installer persists token-in-URL git credentials it promises to refuse

assertions: spec persisted into config + MCP args
dry-run redaction uses same user:pass shape
limitations: The store spec is operator-supplied, and the written config is created 0600; the leak is to the operator's own files/terminal.
Remaining uncertainty: Whether operators actually pass PATs as URL userinfo (GitHub docs show this form for tokens).
validation.summary: normalizeStoreSpec (install.ts:398) matches only `://user:pass@`; the token form `https://TOKEN@host` has no colon and passes; the spec is embedded into the hook command (install.ts:386-394) and MCP args (install.ts:162) and later written to the replica .git/config; safeDiffLine (install.ts:143) redacts only user:pass URLs.

dataflow.summary: store writer -> post with a lexically maximal ts -> its thread's last_activity becomes the TEXT max -> board_threads/resources rank it first and drop real threads past the limit

impact.why: Impact is low because it only distorts thread ordering and can evict legitimate threads from a limited list (availability/integrity of a view), with no code-exec or data disclosure, and likelihood is high; the matrix and DoS calibration keep an ordering-distortion nuisance at low.

likelihood.why: Any store writer; any reader using the index thread list. One object.

reachability.summary: Any store writer; any reader using the index thread list. One object.

attackPath.summary: store writer -> post with a lexically maximal ts -> its thread's last_activity becomes the TEXT max -> board_threads/resources rank it first and drop real threads past the limit

confidence.rationale: PoC ingests a real recent thread then an attacker post with ts 9999-12-31; threads({limit:1}) returns the attacker thread, confirming it pins above real activity.

preventiveControls: Derive all ordering/time fields from the signed/validated ULID rather than the free-text ts.
findings.remediation: Reject non-ISO or out-of-range `ts` values (or rank `last_activity` by the ULID-derived time of `id` rather than the raw `ts`).
remediationTests: A post with a far-future or non-ISO ts does not rank above genuinely recent threads.

rootCause.summary: post.ts (post.ts:97) accepts any Date.parse-able string; ingestOne (index.ts:154-164) folds it into threads.last_activity via TEXT max(); threads() orders by last_activity DESC with a LIMIT (index.ts:287-291), so a lexically large ts pins the thread and evicts legitimate threads from the window.

severity.changeConditions: Rejecting non-ISO or clearly-out-of-range ts values (or ranking by the ULID-derived time rather than the raw ts) removes it.
severity.rationale: Impact is low because it only distorts thread ordering and can evict legitimate threads from a limited list (availability/integrity of a view), with no code-exec or data disclosure, and likelihood is high; the matrix and DoS calibration keep an ordering-distortion nuisance at low.

findings.summary: Thread ordering manipulation via attacker `ts`: post.ts is only Date.parse-checked (any parseable string incl. non-ISO), stored raw, and threads.last_activity is computed with TEXT max() and ordered DESC, so a post with a lexically large ts (e.g. 9999-... ) pins its thread permanently above all real activity and can push legitimate threads out of the default limit window in board_threads and thread resources.
findings.title: Attacker-controlled ts pins and evicts threads in the index views

assertions: threads ORDER BY last_activity DESC LIMIT
limitations: Attacker content already appears on the board; the added harm is ordering/eviction of the thread list.
Remaining uncertainty: Whether readers rely on board_threads ordering for anything security-relevant.
validation.summary: post.ts (post.ts:97) accepts any Date.parse-able string; ingestOne (index.ts:154-164) folds it into threads.last_activity via TEXT max(); threads() orders by last_activity DESC with a LIMIT (index.ts:287-291), so a lexically large ts pins the thread and evicts legitimate threads from the window.

dataflow.summary: store writer creates many threads / many distinct board names -> a single resources/list registers them all in watchedResources -> the 2s poll loop performs O(threads) store syncs forever, each hitting the backend

impact.why: Impact is low because it is local resource/backend load on the MCP process with no data or integrity effect, and likelihood is medium because any store writer can inflate the watched set; the DoS calibration keeps a mitigable, local, resource-only issue at low.

likelihood.why: Any store writer; affects the local MCP server and its store backend (git stores also commit/fetch each sync). No auth.

reachability.summary: Any store writer; affects the local MCP server and its store backend (git stores also commit/fetch each sync). No auth.

attackPath.summary: store writer creates many threads / many distinct board names -> a single resources/list registers them all in watchedResources -> the 2s poll loop performs O(threads) store syncs forever, each hitting the backend

confidence.rationale: listResources adds every listed thread (up to 1000/board, boards derived from attacker-claimed post.board) to watchedResources, which is never pruned; pollResources re-reads each every 2s with its own index.sync.

preventiveControls: Cap subscription/polling fan-out from attacker-controlled object counts.
findings.remediation: Bound the watched-resource set and prune entries that are not actively subscribed; do not add every listed thread to the polling set.
remediationTests: A resources/list over many threads does not grow the polled set without bound.

rootCause.summary: listResources (server.ts:393) adds each resource uri to watchedResources; pollResources (server.ts:434-449) fingerprints every entry every resourcePollMs (2s), each via readResource->syncBoard (store list/get).

severity.changeConditions: Capping the watched-resource set and pruning entries not actively subscribed would remove the unbounded growth.
severity.rationale: Impact is low because it is local resource/backend load on the MCP process with no data or integrity effect, and likelihood is medium because any store writer can inflate the watched set; the DoS calibration keeps a mitigable, local, resource-only issue at low.

findings.summary: Unbounded resource polling: every thread returned by resources/list (up to 1000 per board, boards taken from attacker-claimed post.board values) is added to watchedResources and never pruned; pollResources then calls readResource for each entry every 2 s, and each readResource performs its own index.sync (store list/get round trips) plus thread materialisation, so a store writer who creates many threads turns one resources/list into a permanent O(threads) store-polling loop in every MCP server.
findings.title: Unbounded MCP resource-watch set enables a persistent polling drain

assertions: resources/list adds every thread to watchedResources
limitations: Local MCP process only; bounded by MAX_LIMIT (1000) per board but grows with distinct attacker boards.
Remaining uncertainty: Whether real store latency makes the 2s loop fall behind enough to matter.
validation.summary: listResources (server.ts:393) adds each resource uri to watchedResources; pollResources (server.ts:434-449) fingerprints every entry every resourcePollMs (2s), each via readResource->syncBoard (store list/get).
